pages.name: The filling tank
pages.text: An ideal 318.3 µF capacitor, two metal plates with a thin gap of insulation, sits across a 100 V peak, 50 Hz supply. The arrows in the leads show the current, the charge arriving each second. The charge on the plates follows the voltage, so the current is the [[capacitance]] × the steepness of the short [[tangent]] riding the voltage wave. At 0 ms the voltage crosses zero at its steepest: the plates are filling fastest and the current is at its 10 A peak. Drag the time cursor.
pages.alt: An ideal capacitor on 100 V peak, 50 Hz. At 3.0 ms the voltage is 80.9 V and the current 5.88 A. The current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage. Its reactance is 10 ohms.

pages.name: At the top
pages.task: The cursor is parked at 5 ms, where the voltage is at its 100 V top and the plates are at their fullest. What current flows in the leads at that instant?
pages.why: A capacitor's current follows how fast its voltage is changing, not how big it is. At its top the voltage has stopped rising and not yet started to fall, so for that instant the charge on the plates holds still: the tangent lies flat and the current is 0 A. 10 A is a resistor's rule, the biggest voltage with the biggest current. −10 A comes at 10 ms, where the voltage falls fastest and the plates drain fastest.
pages.alt: An ideal capacitor on 100 V peak, 50 Hz. At 5.0 ms the voltage is 100.0 V and the current 0.00 A. The current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage. Its reactance is 10 ohms.

pages.name: A quarter cycle ahead
pages.text: Now the cursor sweeps one whole 20 ms cycle, tracing the current from the tangent. After its top the voltage falls, the plates drain and the arrows turn round. The bracket marks the 5 ms from the current's top to the voltage's, a quarter cycle: the current [[leads]] and the voltage [[lags]]. Measured as in lesson 4, by how far the voltage leads, that is a [[phase angle]] of −90°. Drag the cursor to follow it.
pages.alt: An ideal capacitor on 100 V peak, 50 Hz. At 20.0 ms the voltage is 0.0 V and the current 10.00 A. The current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage. Its reactance is 10 ohms.

pages.name: Which leads?
pages.task: Here are the capacitor's waves again, standing still. Which leads, and by how much?
pages.answer: The current, by a quarter cycle
pages.why: Read along the time axis. The current tops out at 20 ms and the voltage 5 ms later, at 25 ms. Whichever peaks first is ahead, so the current leads by 5 ms, a quarter of the 20 ms cycle, and the voltage lags by the same: a [[phase angle]] of −90°. The voltage leading is the coil's answer from lesson 4, carried over. Half a cycle, 10 ms, would put the current's top where the voltage has its bottom.
pages.alt: An ideal capacitor on 100 V peak, 50 Hz. The current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage. Its reactance is 10 ohms.

pages.name: A faster supply
pages.text: The frequency plays from 50 Hz up to 100 Hz on the same 100 V peak. The plates still fill to the same charge, but in half the time, so at 0 ms the voltage is twice as steep and the current twice as big. The capacitor's opposition, the voltage ÷ the current, is its [[capacitive reactance]], X_C. It falls as the frequency rises, while lesson 4's X_L climbs. Now slide the frequency yourself.
pages.alt: An ideal capacitor on 100 V peak, 100 Hz. At 0.0 ms the voltage is 0.0 V and the current 20.00 A. The current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage. Its reactance is 5 ohms.

pages.name: On board ship
pages.task: A marine college's notes (a secondary source) give 60 Hz as the frequency most common on board ship. With the same 100 V peak, how high does this capacitor's current peak at 60 Hz?
pages.why: X_C falls as the frequency rises: 10 Ω × 50 ÷ 60 = 8.33 Ω, the same as 1 ÷ (2π × 60 × 0.0003183). The supply's peak is still 100 V, so the current peaks at 100 ÷ 8.33 = 12 A. More frequency means less reactance and more current. 8.33 A is the coil's rule, reactance rising with the frequency, and 10 A leaves the frequency out, as for a resistor.
pages.alt: An ideal capacitor on 100 V peak, 60 Hz. The current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage. Its reactance is 8.33 ohms.

pages.name: Down to steady DC
pages.text: The frequency plays down to 25 Hz: X_C rises to 20 Ω and the current peaks at only 5 A. Follow the X_C curve on towards 0 Hz and it climbs ever more steeply, off the top, while lesson 4's X_L runs down to 0 Ω. Then the supply switches to a steady 100 V. A brief rush of current, only sketched here, fills the plates, and once they are full no more flows: the arrows stay gone at 0 A.
pages.alt: An ideal capacitor on 100 V peak, 25 Hz. On steady DC the plates have filled and no current flows. Its reactance is 20 ohms.

pages.name: The ohmmeter
pages.task: An ohmmeter's reading across a healthy capacitor climbs while it fills and settles very high. Yet on 50 Hz this one lets 10 A peak flow for a 100 V peak. Why the difference?
pages.answer: A steady voltage fills it once, then drives no more current
pages.why: An ohmmeter makes its reading with a small steady voltage. That fills the plates once, and then the charge holds still, so no more current flows and the reading settles very high: the 0 Hz end of the X_C curve. On 50 Hz the voltage never stops changing, so the plates fill and empty every cycle and current keeps flowing in the leads, with 10 Ω of reactance. An open-circuit capacitor would read high too, but it would pass nothing on 50 Hz either, and this one passes 10 A peak; its reading climbs rather than sitting high from the start because the plates are filling. Next to no charge crosses the gap: the current comes from filling and emptying.
pages.alt: An ideal capacitor on 100 V peak, 50 Hz. The current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage. Its reactance is 10 ohms.

pages.name: Taking and giving back
pages.text: Back at 50 Hz, the power wave is the voltage × the current at each instant, as in lesson 3. From 0 to 5 ms both are positive and the plates fill: the dot climbs to 500 W as energy goes in. From 5 to 10 ms the plates drain and the current is negative: the dot dips to −500 W as the energy comes back. It averages 0 W, where lesson 3's heater averages 500 W. The last two rows give OpenStax's memory aid for the coil and the capacitor, ELI the ICE man.
pages.alt: An ideal capacitor on 100 V peak, 50 Hz. At 10.0 ms the voltage is 0.0 V and the current −10.00 A. The current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage. Its reactance is 10 ohms.

pages.name: Mixed: a 100 µF capacitor
pages.task: Mixed. An example 100 µF capacitor goes on 230 V, 50 Hz mains. What current does it draw?
pages.why: First its reactance: X_C = 1 ÷ (2π × 50 × 0.0001) ≈ 31.8 Ω, with 100 µF written as 0.0001 F. Then 230 V ÷ 31.8 Ω = 7.23 A. 2.3 A puts the 100 µF in as if it were 100 Ω. 0 A treats the capacitor as blocking current, as it does once filled on steady DC; on AC it fills and empties every cycle.
pages.alt: A capacitor on 230 V, 50 Hz mains. The current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage. Its reactance is 31.8 ohms.

pages.name: Mixed: a slower supply
pages.task: Mixed. The same 318.3 µF capacitor goes on a 25 Hz supply with the same 100 V peak. What does its current do?
pages.why: Half the frequency doubles the reactance: 10 Ω × 50 ÷ 25 = 20 Ω, so the current peaks at 100 ÷ 20 = 5 A. It still leads by a quarter cycle, 10 ms at 25 Hz, because the current still peaks where the voltage is steepest, at any frequency. 20 A scales the coil's way, and an ideal capacitor's current is never in step with its voltage.
pages.alt: An ideal capacitor on 100 V peak, 25 Hz. The current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage. Its reactance is 20 ohms.

pages.name: Mixed: a mains capacitor
pages.task: Mixed. An ideal capacitor draws 2 A from 230 V, 50 Hz mains, so its X_C is 115 Ω. What does it draw on a 230 V, 60 Hz supply, and what power does it average?
pages.why: X_C falls as the frequency rises: 115 Ω × 50 ÷ 60 ≈ 95.8 Ω, so the current is 230 ÷ 95.8 = 2.4 A. An ideal capacitor still stores energy as it fills and hands it all back as it empties, so it averages 0 W. 1.67 A scales the current down, as for a coil, and 230 × 2.4 = 552 is volts × amps, which for a capacitor is not watts.
pages.alt: An ideal capacitor on 230 V, 60 Hz. The current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage. Its reactance is 95.8 ohms.
